title: Book 10
paragraphs: Let me know you, Lord, you who already know me — let me know you as I am known by you. Power of my soul, enter into it and make it fit for you, so that you may have and hold it without stain or blemish. This is my hope, and that is why I speak; and it is in this hope that I rejoice, when my rejoicing is healthy. As for the other things of this life, the more they are grieved over the less they deserve it, and the less they are grieved over the more they deserve it. For see — you love the truth, and whoever does the truth comes to the light. This is what I want to do in my heart before you in confession, and in this writing, before many witnesses.

And from you, Lord, to whose eyes the abyss of a man's conscience lies bare, what could be hidden in me even if I refused to confess it? I would only be hiding you from myself, not myself from you. But now, because my groaning bears witness that I am displeased with myself, you shine out, and you are pleasing and beloved and longed for, so that I may be ashamed of myself and renounce myself and choose you, pleasing neither you nor myself except in you. To you, then, Lord, I am open, whatever I am; and I have already said what fruit comes from my confessing to you. I do not do it with words and sounds of the flesh but with the words of the soul and the cry of the mind, which your ear knows. For when I am in the wrong, to confess to you is nothing else than to be displeased with myself; and when I am holy, it is nothing else than not to credit myself with it — because you, Lord, bless the godly, but you first justify the ungodly. My confession, then, my God, is made in your sight silently and not silently. In sound it is silent; in feeling it cries aloud. For I say nothing right to men that you have not already heard from me, and you hear nothing from me that you did not first say to me.

What then do I have to do with men, that they should hear my confessions — as if they could heal all my weaknesses — a race curious to know other people's lives, but too lazy to correct their own? Why do they want to hear from me what I am, when they will not hear from you what they themselves are? And when they hear about myself from me, how do they know whether I am telling the truth — since no one knows what is in a man except the spirit of the man that is in him? But if they hear from you about themselves, they cannot say, "The Lord is lying." For what is it to hear from you about themselves, but to know themselves? And who knows this and says, "It is false," unless he himself is lying? But because love believes all things — at least among those whom it binds to itself and makes one — I too, Lord, will confess to you in such a way that men may hear, even though I cannot prove to them whether I confess truly; yet those whose ears love has opened to me will believe me.

But you, my innermost Physician, make plain to me what fruit I may gain by doing this. The confessions of my past sins — which you have forgiven and covered over, so that you might make me happy in you, changing my soul through faith and your sacrament — when read and heard, stir the heart so that it does not sleep in despair and say, "I cannot," but wakes in the love of your mercy and the sweetness of your grace, by which the weak becomes strong, once he has become aware of his own weakness through it. And good people are glad to hear of the past evils of those who are now free of them — not because they are evils, but because they were and now are not. With what fruit, then, Lord my God — to whom my conscience confesses daily, trusting more in the hope of your mercy than in its own innocence — with what fruit, I ask, do I confess to men also, in your presence, through this book, what I now am, not what I have been? That other fruit I have already seen and spoken of. But what I now am, at this very moment of making these confessions, is what many want to know — those who have known me or have not, those who have heard from me or heard about me — but their ear is not at my heart, where I am, whatever I am. They want, then, to hear me confess what I am within, where neither their eye nor their ear nor their understanding can reach; they want it, ready to believe me — but will they actually know? For the love by which they are good tells them that I do not lie in my confessions, and that love in them believes me.

But to what end would they hear this? Do they want to rejoice with me when they hear how close, by your gift, I have drawn to you? And to pray for me when they hear how much I am held back by my own weight? To such people I will reveal myself. For it is no small fruit, Lord my God, that many should give thanks to you on our behalf, and that many should entreat you for us. Let the brotherly mind love in me what you teach is to be loved, and grieve in me what you teach is to be grieved over. Let it be a brotherly mind, not the mind of a stranger — not that of the strange children whose mouth speaks emptiness and whose right hand is a right hand of wickedness — but the brotherly mind which, when it approves, rejoices for me, and when it disapproves, grieves for me; because whether it approves or disapproves, it loves me. To such people I will reveal myself. They will breathe freely at my good deeds and sigh at my bad ones. My good deeds are your doing and your gifts; my evil ones are my own offenses and your judgments on them. Let them breathe freely at the one and sigh at the other, and let hymns and weeping rise up into your sight out of the hearts of my brothers, your censers. And may you, Lord, be pleased with the incense of your holy temple; have mercy on me according to your great mercy, for your own name's sake; and never abandoning what you have begun, bring my unfinished parts to completion.

This is the fruit of my confessions about what I am, not about what I have been — to confess this, not only before you, in a secret exultation mixed with trembling, and a secret sorrow mixed with hope, but also in the ears of the believing children of men, who share my joy and share my mortality with me, my fellow citizens and fellow pilgrims, those who have gone ahead and those who are yet to follow, companions on my way. These are your servants, my brothers, whom you want to be your sons; my masters, whom you command me to serve if I want to live with you, from you. But this word of yours would count for little if it only commanded by speaking and did not go ahead of me in doing. This, then, I do in deed and in word; this I do under your wings — in too great a danger, if my soul were not subdued to you under your wings, and my weakness known to you. I am a little one, but my Father lives forever, and my Guardian is sufficient for me. For he is the same one who begot me and who defends me, and you yourself are all my good — you, the Almighty, who are with me, indeed before I am with you. To those, then, whom you command me to serve, I will reveal not what I have been but what I now am and what I still am. But I do not judge myself either. This, then, is how I wish to be heard.

For you, Lord, judge me — because although no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him, still there is something in a man which even the spirit of the man that is in him does not itself know. But you, Lord, know everything about him, since you made him. Yet even I, though in your sight I despise myself and count myself dust and ashes, even I know something of you that I do not know of myself. And it is true that we now see through a glass, darkly, not yet face to face. So then, as long as I am away from you, I am more present to myself than I am to you; and yet I know that you cannot suffer or be changed, while I do not know what temptations I can resist and what I cannot. And there is hope, because you are faithful, and will not let us be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, but with the temptation will also make a way of escape, so that we may be able to endure it. I will confess, then, what I know of myself; I will confess also what I do not know of myself. And this because what I do know of myself I know by your shining upon me, and what I do not know of myself I remain ignorant of until my darkness is made like noonday in your presence.

Not with doubt but with assured awareness do I love you, Lord. You have struck my heart with your word, and I loved you. And also heaven and earth and everything in them, look — on every side they urge me to love you, and they never stop saying so to everyone, so that no one has an excuse. But you will have mercy more deeply on whom you will have mercy, and will have compassion on whom you have had compassion; otherwise heaven and earth speak your praises to deaf ears. But what do I love, when I love you? Not the beauty of bodies, nor the fair rhythm of time, nor the brightness of light so pleasant to our eyes, nor the sweet melodies of varied songs, nor the fragrant smell of flowers and ointments and spices, not manna and honey, not limbs welcoming to the embraces of the flesh. None of these do I love when I love my God; and yet I do love a kind of light, and a kind of melody, and a kind of fragrance, and a kind of food, and a kind of embrace, when I love my God — the light, the melody, the fragrance, the food, the embrace of my inner self, where there shines for my soul what no space can contain, and where there sounds what no time sweeps away, and where there is a fragrance that no breathing scatters, and where there is a taste that no eating lessens, and where there is a clinging that no fullness pulls apart. This is what I love when I love my God.

And what is this that I love? I asked the earth, and it answered me, "I am not him"; and everything in it confessed the same. I asked the sea and the depths and the living, creeping things, and they answered, "We are not your God, seek above us." I asked the moving air, and the whole air with everything that lives in it answered, "Anaximenes was wrong, I am not God." I asked the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars: "Nor are we the God you are seeking," they said. And I said to all the things that surround the door of my flesh, "You have told me about my God, that you are not him — tell me something about him." And they cried out in a loud voice, "He made us." My questioning them was my thinking about them, and their beautiful form was their answer. And I turned toward myself and said to myself, "Who are you?" And I answered, "A man." And look — in me there present themselves to me a soul and a body, one outward, the other inward. By which of these ought I to seek my God? I had sought him in the body, from earth to heaven, as far as I could send out messengers — the rays of my eyes. But the better part is the inner one, since to it, as presiding judge, all the bodily messengers reported the answers of heaven and earth and everything in them, which said, "We are not God, but he made us." My inner self knew these things through the service of the outer; I, the inner one, knew them — I, the mind, through the senses of my body. I asked the whole framework of the world about my God, and it answered me, "I am not him, but he made me."

Is this bodily shape not plain to everyone whose senses are sound? Why then does it not speak the same thing to everyone? Animals large and small see it, but they cannot question it, because no reason is set over their senses to judge on what they report. But men can question it, so that the invisible things of God are clearly seen, understood through the things that are made; yet by loving these things, men become subject to them, and subjects cannot judge. Nor do created things answer those who ask, unless the askers can judge; nor do they change their voice — that is, their appearance — if one person merely looks while another looks and questions, so as to appear one way to this one and another way to that one; rather, appearing the same way to both, it is silent to one and speaks to the other — or rather, it speaks to all, but only those understand who compare the voice it gives from outside with the truth within. For truth says to me, "Neither heaven, nor earth, nor any other body is your God." This their very nature tells anyone who looks at them: "We are a mass, and a mass is smaller in a part of itself than in the whole." Now I speak to you, my soul: you are my better part, for you give life to the mass of my body, giving it what no body can give to a body. But your God is, for you too, the life of your life.

What then do I love, when I love my God? Who is he, above the summit of my soul? By way of my very soul I will climb up to him. I will pass beyond that power by which I am joined to my body and fill its whole frame with life. But I cannot find my God by that power, for then a horse and a mule, which have no understanding, could find him too, since it is the same power by which even their bodies live. But there is another power in me — not just the one by which I give life, but the one by which I give my flesh its senses, the flesh the Lord shaped for me — commanding the eye not to hear and the ear not to see, but giving the eye the task of seeing through it and the ear the task of hearing through it, and to each of the other senses its own proper place and office; and although these are different, it is I, the one mind, who act through all of them. I will pass beyond this power of mine as well, for the horse and the mule have this too, since they also perceive through the body.

I will pass, then, beyond this power of my nature as well, rising by stages toward him who made me. And I come to the fields and vast palaces of my memory, where the treasures of countless images are stored, images brought in from things of every kind perceived by the senses. Stored there too is whatever else we think about, whether by enlarging or diminishing or in any other way varying the things the senses have reached; and whatever else has been entrusted to it and laid up there, and which forgetfulness has not yet swallowed and buried. When I enter there, I ask for whatever I want brought forward, and some things come at once; others must be searched for longer, and are fetched out as if from some inner storeroom; others rush out in crowds, and while one thing is wanted and asked for, they leap forward as if to say, "Could it be me?" These I wave away with the hand of my heart, from the face of my remembering, until what I am looking for is unveiled and comes into view out of its hiding place. Other things present themselves readily, in unbroken order, just as they are called for, those in front making way for those that follow, and as they make way, they slip out of sight, ready to come again when I want them. All of this happens when I recite something from memory.

All these things are kept distinct and under their own general headings, each having come in by its own entrance: light and all the colors and shapes of bodies by the eyes, every kind of sound by the ears, every smell by way of the nostrils, every taste by the mouth, and by the sensation of the whole body what is hard or soft, hot or cold, rough or smooth, heavy or light, whether outside the body or within it. All these that great harbor of the memory receives, in its countless secret and indescribable passages, to be brought forward again when needed, each entering by its own gate and laid up there. And yet the things themselves do not enter in — only the images of the things perceived are there, ready for thought to call back. Who can say how these images are formed, even though it is plain enough by which sense each one was brought in and stored? For even while I sit in darkness and silence, in my memory I can bring up colors if I want to, and tell black from white, and whichever others I choose; nor do sounds break in and disturb the image taken in by my eyes, which I am looking over again, even though they too are there, lying dormant and laid up as if set apart. For I can call for these too, and at once they appear. And though my tongue is still and my throat silent, I can sing as much as I want; and those images of colors, which are there all the same, do not push themselves forward and interrupt when another store is called for, the one that flowed in through the ears. In the same way I recall at will the other things piled up by the other senses. I can tell the scent of lilies from violets even while smelling nothing, and I prefer honey to sweet wine, and smooth to rough, at a time when I am neither tasting nor touching anything, but only remembering.

All this I do within, in that vast court of my memory. There I have present with me heaven, earth, sea, and whatever I can think of in them, besides what I have forgotten. There too I meet myself, and recall myself — what I have done, when, where, and in what state of mind. There is everything I remember, whether from my own experience or on someone else's word. Out of that same storehouse I myself combine fresh likenesses, again and again, with things past, out of what I have experienced or, from what I have experienced, come to believe; and from these I go on to infer future actions, events, and hopes, and I reflect on all of these too as though they were present. "I will do this or that," I say to myself, in that great storehouse of my mind, filled with the images of so many great things, "and this or that will follow." "If only this or that could happen!" "God keep this or that from happening!" So I speak to myself, and when I speak, the images of everything I speak of are present, out of that same treasury of memory; and I would not be able to speak of any of it if the images were missing.

Great is this power of memory, immensely great, my God — a vast and boundless inner chamber! Who has ever reached the bottom of it? Yet this is a power that belongs to me, part of my own nature, and I myself do not grasp the whole of what I am. So then the mind is too small to contain itself. But where would that be, the part of itself it does not contain? Is it outside itself, and not within? How then does it not grasp itself? A great wonder seizes me over this, astonishment takes hold of me. Men go out to marvel at the heights of mountains, the huge waves of the sea, the broad flow of rivers, the vastness of the ocean, and the wheeling of the stars, and they pass by themselves without wondering; nor are they amazed that when I spoke of all these things just now, I was not seeing them with my eyes, and yet I could not have spoken of them unless I actually saw, inwardly, in my memory, the mountains, the waves, the rivers, the stars which I had seen, and the ocean which I believe exists — and saw them there with the same vast distances between them as if I were seeing them outside myself. Yet it was not by seeing them that I drew them into myself when I looked at them with my eyes; they themselves are not with me, only their images are. And I know by which bodily sense each one was impressed on me.

Yet the immeasurable capacity of my memory holds not only these things. Here too is everything I have learned from the liberal arts and not yet forgotten, moved as it were to some inner place which is nevertheless no place at all; and these are not images of the things, but the things themselves. For whatever I know of literature, of the art of argument, of how many kinds of questions there are — all of it exists in my memory in such a way that I have not simply taken in an image and left the thing itself out, or as though it had sounded and passed away like a voice fixed on the ear by that imprint, by which it might be recalled as though still sounding when it no longer sounds; or as a smell, while it passes and evaporates into the air, affects the sense of smell, from which it carries into the memory an image of itself, which we renew when we remember; or as food, which truly in the stomach now has no taste, and yet in the memory still in a sense tastes; or as anything the body perceives by touch, which the memory still forms an idea of even after it has been taken away from us. For these things are not carried into the memory themselves — only their images are caught up with astonishing speed and stored as it were in wonderful cabinets, and from there wonderfully brought forth again by the act of remembering.

Now when I hear that there are three kinds of questions — "whether a thing exists? what it is? what kind of thing it is?" — I do hold onto the images of the sounds that make up those words, and I know that those sounds passed through the air with a noise and now are gone. But the things themselves that are meant by those sounds I never reached with any bodily sense, nor ever perceived them except in my mind; yet in my memory I have stored not images of them but the things themselves. How they got into me, let them explain if they can, for I have gone over every entryway of my flesh and cannot find which one they came in by. The eyes say, "If they had color, we reported them." The ears say, "If they made a sound, we gave notice of them." The nostrils say, "If they had a smell, they passed by us." Taste says, "Unless they have a flavor, do not ask me." Touch says, "If it has no size, I did not handle it; if I did not handle it, I gave no report of it." From where, then, and how did these things get into my memory? I do not know how. For when I learned them, I did not simply trust someone else's mind — I recognized them in my own, and finding them true, I entrusted them to my memory, laying them up as it were where I could bring them out again when I wanted. So they were in my heart even before I learned them, but not yet in my memory. Where, then, were they? And why, when they were spoken, did I recognize them and say, "Yes, that is so, that is true," unless they were already in the memory, but pushed back and buried, as it were, in deeper recesses — so deep that, if someone else's prompting had not drawn them out, I might perhaps have been unable to conceive of them at all?

So we find that to learn these things — things whose images we do not absorb through our senses, but which we perceive within, in themselves, without images, just as they are — is nothing other than this: by understanding, to take hold of them, and by paying attention, to see to it that the things the memory already held, but at random and unsorted, are laid up ready to hand, as it were, in that same memory where before they lay unknown, scattered, and neglected — so that they now come readily to a mind already familiar with them. And how many things of this kind does my memory carry, things already discovered and, as I said, placed as it were within reach, things we are said to have learned and come to know — which, if I were to stop calling them to mind for even a short time, sink back and slip again, as it were, into deeper recesses, so that they must be thought out again from there as if new, for they have no other dwelling place; they must be gathered together again so that they can be known, that is, collected once more out of their scattered state — which is where the word "cogitation" comes from. For cogo ("I gather") and cogito ("I gather again," i.e. think) stand to each other as ago does to agito, and facio to factito. But the mind has claimed this word, cogitation, for its own use, so that not whatever is gathered anywhere, but what is gathered again — brought together — in the mind, is properly said to be cogitated, or thought upon.

The memory also holds countless principles and laws of numbers and of dimensions, none of which has been imprinted by any bodily sense, since they have no color, no sound, no taste, no smell, no touch. I have heard the sound of the words by which they are named when discussed, but the sounds are one thing and the things another. For the sounds differ between Greek and Latin, but the things themselves are neither Greek nor Latin nor any other language. I have seen the lines drawn by architects, the finest of them, as fine as a spider's thread, but these are still different — they are not the images of those lines that the eye of flesh showed me; whoever recognizes them within himself, without any thought of a body at all, knows them for what they are. I have also perceived the numbers by which we count the things we sense with our bodies, but the numbers by which we count are different, and they are not images of those sensed things, and so they truly exist in their own right. Let whoever does not see this mock me for saying so, and I will pity him even as he mocks me.

I remember all these things, and I remember how I learned them. I also remember having heard many objections falsely raised against them, and even though the objections are false, it is not false that I remember them; and I remember too that I have distinguished between those truths and the falsehoods raised against them. And I see that my present grasp of these distinctions is different from remembering that I have often made them before, when I often thought them through. So I both remember having often understood these things, and I lay up in my memory what I now discern and understand, so that afterward I may remember that I understand it now. So then I also remember having remembered — just as, if later on I recall that I have now been able to remember these things, it will be by the power of memory that I call it to mind.

That same memory also holds the feelings of my mind — not in the way the mind itself holds them when it feels them, but quite differently, according to a power all its own. For without rejoicing I remember that I once rejoiced, and without sorrow I recall a past sorrow of mine. And what I once feared I look back on without fear, and I call to mind a past desire without desiring it now. Sometimes, on the other hand, I remember a past sorrow of mine with joy, and a past joy with sorrow. This is not strange when it concerns the body, since the mind is one thing and the body another; if I remember some past bodily pain with joy, that is not so strange. But now, since this very memory is itself mind — for when we tell someone to keep a thing in memory, we say, "See that you keep it in mind," and when we forget something, we say, "It did not come to my mind," or "It slipped out of my mind," calling the memory itself the mind — this being so, how is it that when I remember my past sorrow with joy, the mind has joy while the memory has sorrow; the mind is joyful over the gladness that is in it, and yet the memory, over the sadness that is in it, is not sad? Does the memory perhaps not belong to the mind? Who would say that? The memory, then, is like the stomach of the mind, and joy and sorrow are like sweet and bitter food, which, once committed to the memory, pass as it were into the stomach, where they can be stored but no longer tasted. It is absurd to picture these as truly alike, and yet they are not wholly unlike either.

And yet, look — it is out of my memory that I bring it forth when I say there are four disturbances of the mind: desire, joy, fear, sorrow; and whatever I can argue about them, dividing each into its subordinate kinds and defining it, I find in my memory what to say, and from there I bring it out; yet I am not disturbed by any of these feelings when I call them to mind and remember them — indeed, before I recalled and brought them back, they were already there, and that is why they could be brought back by recollection. Perhaps, then, just as food is brought up from the stomach by chewing the cud, so these are brought up from the memory by recollection. Why then does the one arguing about them, in the very act of recollecting, not taste in the mouth of his musing the sweetness of joy, or the bitterness of sorrow? Is the comparison unlike at this point, because it is not alike in every respect? For who would be willing to speak of these things at all, if every time we named grief or fear we were forced to feel sad or afraid? And yet we could not speak of them at all if we did not find in our memory not only the sounds of their names, following the images stamped there by the bodily senses, but also notions of the very things themselves, which we never received through any bodily channel at all, but which the mind itself, perceiving them through the experience of its own inner states, entrusted to the memory, or which the memory retained of itself, without having been given them.

But whether by images or not, who can easily say? For instance, I name a stone, I name the sun, when the things themselves are not present to my senses, but their images are present to my memory. I name a bodily pain, and yet it is not present to me when nothing hurts; still, unless its image were present in my memory, I would not know what to say about it, nor could I, in discussing it, tell pain from pleasure. I name bodily health; being healthy in body, the thing itself is present with me; yet unless its image too were present in my memory, I could in no way recall what the sound of this name should mean. Nor would a sick person, hearing health named, recognize what was meant, unless the same image were retained by the power of memory, even though the thing itself were absent from the body. I name the numbers by which we count, and it is not their images but the numbers themselves that are present in my memory. I name the image of the sun, and that image is present in my memory — for I do not call up the image of its image, but the image itself is present to me when I call it to mind. I name memory, and I recognize what I am naming. But where do I recognize it, except in the memory itself? Is it present to itself by way of its image, then, and not by itself?

What about when I name forgetfulness, and recognize what I am naming even then? How could I recognize it if I did not remember it? I do not mean the sound of the name, but the thing it signifies — which, if I had forgotten it, I could not recognize what that sound means. So when I remember memory, memory itself is present to itself through itself; but when I remember forgetfulness, both memory and forgetfulness are present — memory, by which I remember, and forgetfulness, which I remember. But what is forgetfulness except the absence of memory? How then can it be present so that I remember it, when, once present, it would prevent me from remembering at all? But if what we remember, we hold in memory, and yet unless we remembered forgetfulness we could never, on hearing the name, recognize the thing it signifies, then forgetfulness must be retained by memory. So it is present in order that we not forget, and being present in that way, we forget. From this we must understand that forgetfulness, when we remember it, is not present to the memory in itself but through its image — because if it were present in itself, it would cause us not to remember but to forget. Who, now, can search this out? Who can grasp how this can be?

Lord, I truly struggle over this — I struggle within myself. I have become a difficult soil that demands hard labor and much sweat. For we are not now searching out the regions of the sky, or measuring the distances of the stars, or asking after the balance of the earth. It is I myself who remember — I, the mind. It would not be so strange if what I myself am not were far from me. But what is nearer to me than myself? And yet, look — the power of my own memory is not understood by me, even though I cannot so much as name myself without it. For what am I to say, when it is plain to me that I remember forgetfulness? Should I say that what I remember is not in my memory? Or should I say that forgetfulness is in my memory for the very purpose that I might not forget? Both would be utterly absurd. What third possibility is there? How can I say that it is the image of forgetfulness that is retained by my memory, and not forgetfulness itself, when I remember it? How could I even say this, seeing that whenever the image of a thing is stamped on the memory, the thing itself must first have been present, so that its image could be stamped there? This is how I remember Carthage, and all the places I have been, and the faces of men I have seen, and things reported by the other senses — this is how I remember the health or sickness of the body. For when these things were present, my memory took images from them, images which, being present with me, I could look upon and bring back in my mind when I remembered the things themselves in their absence. If, then, this forgetfulness is retained in the memory through its image and not through itself, then clearly it must itself once have been present, so that its image could be taken. But when it was present, how did it write its image into the memory, since forgetfulness, by its very presence, wipes out even what it finds already recorded there? And yet, however this may be — even though the way of it is beyond conceiving and beyond explaining — I am certain that I do remember forgetfulness itself, the very thing by which what we remember is wiped away.

Great is the power of memory — something to be in awe of, my God — a deep and boundless multiplicity; and this thing is the mind, and this is myself. What then am I, my God? What kind of nature am I? A life various and manifold and immensely vast. Look — in the plains and caves and caverns of my memory, countless and countlessly full of countless kinds of things, whether through images, as with all bodies, or through their actual presence, as with the arts, or through certain notions or impressions, as with the feelings of the mind, which the memory retains even when the mind itself does not feel them, though whatever is in the memory is also in the mind — over all of these I run, I fly, I dive this way and that, as far as I am able, and there is no end to it. So great is the power of memory, so great the force of life, even in the mortal life of man. What then shall I do, you who are my true life, my God? I will pass even beyond this power of mine that is called memory — yes, I will pass beyond it, so that I may draw near to you, O sweet Light. What do you say to me? See, I am climbing up through my mind toward you, who remain above me. Yes, I will now pass beyond this power of mine that is called memory, longing to reach you, the one by whom you can be reached, and to cling to you, the one by whom one can cling to you. For even beasts and birds have memory — otherwise they could not find their way back to their dens and nests, nor manage the many other things they are accustomed to; indeed, they could not be accustomed to anything at all except by memory. So I will pass beyond memory too, so that I may reach him who has set me apart from the four-footed beasts and made me wiser than the birds of the air — I will pass beyond memory too, and where shall I find you, you who are truly good and certain sweetness? And where shall I find you? If I find you outside my memory, then I do not hold you in my memory. And how shall I find you, if I do not remember you at all?

Consider the woman who had lost her coin and searched for it with a lamp — unless she had remembered it, she would never have found it. For once it was found, how would she know it was the same coin unless she remembered it? I remember having searched for and found many things, and I know this because when I was looking for one of them and was asked, "Is this it?" "Is that it?" I kept saying "No," until the thing I was looking for was offered to me. And if I had not remembered it, whatever it was, even if it had been offered to me I would not have found it, because I could not have recognized it. And this is always how it is when we search for and find something that was lost. Yet when something is lost merely from sight, not from memory — some visible body, say — its image is still retained within, and it is searched for until it is restored to sight, and when it is found, it is recognized by the image that is within; nor do we say we have found what was lost unless we recognize it, and we cannot recognize it unless we remember it. But this was lost to the eyes, while it was kept in the memory.

But what about when memory itself loses something, as happens when we forget and try to recollect? Where, in the end, do we search, if not in the memory itself? And there, if one thing happens to be offered instead of another, we reject it, until the thing we are looking for meets us, and when it does, we say, "This is it" — which we would not say unless we recognized it, and we could not recognize it unless we remembered it. So we had certainly forgotten it. Or was it not that the whole thing had escaped us, but that, holding onto the part we still had, we searched for the part that was lost — because the memory sensed that it was not carrying along everything it was used to carrying, and, crippled as it were by this break in its old habit, demanded back what it was missing? For instance, if we see or think of someone we know, and, having forgotten his name, try to recover it, whatever else comes to mind does not attach itself to it, because it was not used to being thought of together with him, and so it is rejected, until the right name presents itself, the one on which our knowledge settles comfortably as its accustomed object. And where does that name present itself from, if not out of the memory itself? For even when we recognize it because someone else has reminded us, it still comes from there. We do not take it in as something new, but on recollecting it, we acknowledge that what was named is correct. But if it had been utterly wiped from the mind, we would not remember it even when reminded, since we have not yet utterly forgotten what we remember ourselves to have forgotten. Whatever we have utterly forgotten, then, even though it is lost, we cannot even go looking for it.

How then do I seek you, Lord? For when I seek you, my God, I am seeking a happy life. I will seek you so that my soul may live. For my body lives by my soul, and my soul lives by you. How then do I seek a happy life, since I do not have it, until I can say, where I ought to say it, "It is enough"? How do I seek it? By remembering it, as though I had forgotten it, remembering that I had forgotten it? Or by wanting to learn it as something unknown, either never having known it, or having forgotten it so completely that I do not even remember having forgotten it? Is a happy life not what everyone wants, with no one at all failing to want it? Where have they come to know it, that they want it so? Where have they seen it, that they love it so? We truly have it, somehow, though I do not know how. Yes, there is another way too, in which, when someone has it, he is then happy; and there are those who are blessed in hope. These have it in a lesser way than those who have it in reality, yet they are better off than those who are happy neither in reality nor in hope. Yet even these, if they did not have it in some sense, would not want to be happy the way they do — and that they do want this is beyond question. They have come to know it, then, somehow, I do not know how, and so they have it by some kind of knowledge, though what kind I do not know, and I am puzzled whether it is in the memory — for if it is, then we have been happy once, whether each of us individually, or in that man who first sinned, in whom we all died, and from whom we are all born into misery — I am not asking that now, but only this: is the happy life in the memory? For we would not love it if we did not know it. We hear the name, and we all admit that we desire the thing itself, since it is not the mere sound that delights us. For when a Greek hears the word in Latin, he is not delighted, since he does not know what is being said; but we who speak Latin are delighted, and so would he be too, if he heard it in Greek — because the thing itself is neither Greek nor Latin, and it is what Greeks and Latins and speakers of every other language long for so earnestly. It is known, then, to everyone, since if they were all asked with one voice, "Would you like to be happy?" they would answer without hesitation, "We would." And this could not happen unless the thing itself, of which this is the name, were retained in their memory.

But is it the way one remembers Carthage, having seen it? No. For a happy life is not seen with the eye, since it is not a body. Is it, then, the way we remember numbers? No. For whoever has numbers in his knowledge does not go on seeking further to attain them; but a happy life we already have in our knowledge, and that is exactly why we love it, and yet we still long to attain it, so that we may be happy. Is it, then, the way we remember eloquence? No. For although, on hearing this name too, some call the thing to mind who are still not yet eloquent, and many who wish to be so — which shows that it is in their knowledge — yet these have observed others being eloquent through their bodily senses, and have been delighted, and desire to be like them, though indeed they would not be delighted unless they had some inward knowledge of it, nor would they wish to be like it unless that delight came from something within; whereas a happy life we do not experience in others by any bodily sense at all. Is it, then, the way we remember joy? Perhaps — for I remember my own joy even when I am sad, just as I remember a happy life even when I am unhappy; nor did I ever see, hear, smell, taste, or touch my joy with any bodily sense, but I experienced it in my mind when I rejoiced, and the knowledge of it clung to my memory, so that I can call it back sometimes with distaste, at other times with longing, depending on the nature of the things in which I remember having rejoiced. For even from shameful things I have at times been submerged in a kind of joy, which now, recalling it, I detest and curse; at other times from good and honest things, which I recall with longing, even though they may no longer be present — and so it is with sadness that I recall a former joy.

Where, then, and when did I experience my happy life, that I should remember it and love it and long for it? It is not I alone, or a few others besides me, but all of us want to be happy — and unless we knew this by some sure knowledge, we would not desire it with such a sure will. But how can it be that if two men are asked whether they would go to war, one might answer that he would, and the other that he would not, while if they were asked whether they would like to be happy, both would say at once, without any hesitation, that they would — and for no other reason would the one go to war and the other refuse, except to be happy. Is it, perhaps, that just as one person looks for his joy in one thing and another in another, they all agree in wanting to be happy, just as they would agree, if asked, that they want to have joy, and this joy is what they call a happy life? So then, although one person obtains this joy by one means and another by another, all have a single goal they strive to reach, namely joy — and since this is something everyone must admit having experienced, it is therefore found in the memory, and recognized whenever the name of a happy life is mentioned.

Far be it, Lord, far be it from the heart of your servant who confesses here to you — far be it that, whatever the joy may be, I should on that account think myself happy. For there is a joy that is not given to the ungodly, but only to those who love you for your own sake, whose joy you yourself are. And this is the happy life: to rejoice toward you, of you, for you; this is it, and there is no other. For those who think there is another kind pursue some other joy, and not the true one. Yet even so, their will is not turned away entirely from some semblance of joy.

It is not certain, then, that everyone wishes to be happy, since those who do not wish to rejoice in you — which is the only happy life — do not truly desire the happy life at all. Or do all men desire it, but because the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, so that they cannot do what they would, do they fall back on what they can do, and settle for that — because what they are not able to do, they do not will strongly enough to make themselves able to do it? For let me ask anyone: would he rather rejoice in truth, or in falsehood? People will no more hesitate to say "in truth" than they would to say that they want to be happy, since a happy life is joy in the truth — that is, joy in you, who are the Truth, O God my light, the health of my countenance, my God. This is the happy life that everyone desires; this life, which alone is happy, everyone desires; to rejoice in the truth, everyone desires. I have met many who would deceive others, but no one who wants to be deceived. Where, then, did they come to know this happy life, if not in the very place where they know the truth as well? For they love the truth too, since they would not want to be deceived. And when they love a happy life, which is nothing other than rejoicing in the truth, then they also love the truth — which they could not love at all, if there were not some notice of it in their memory. Why then do they not rejoice in it? Why are they not happy? Because they are more strongly taken up with other things that have more power to make them miserable than the truth they so faintly remember has power to make them happy. For there is still a little light in men; let them walk, let them walk, so that darkness does not overtake them.

But why does "truth breed hatred," and why does a man of yours who preaches the truth become their enemy? A happy life, after all, is loved, and it is nothing other than rejoicing in the truth — so is it not that truth is loved in this qualified way, that those who love something else would gladly have whatever they love be the truth, and, since they do not want to be deceived, refuse to be convinced that they are? So they hate the truth for the sake of the very thing they loved in place of the truth. They love truth when it shines a light for them, and hate it when it convicts them. For since they do not want to be deceived themselves, yet want to deceive others, they love truth when it reveals itself to them, and hate it when it reveals them. And so it repays them in a way that fits: those who refuse to be shown up by it, it exposes against their will, while it does not show itself to them in return. This, yes, this is how the mind of man behaves — blind and sick, foul and disfigured as it is — wanting to stay hidden, but wanting nothing hidden from it. Yet it receives the opposite of what it wants: it is not hidden from the Truth, while the Truth is hidden from it. And yet, even in this miserable state, it would still rather rejoice in truths than in falsehoods. It will be happy, then, when, with no distraction standing in the way, it rejoices in that one Truth alone, by whom all things are true.

See what a distance I have traveled through my memory seeking you, Lord — and I have not found you outside of it. For I have found nothing about you except what I have kept in memory ever since I first learned you. Since I learned you, I have not forgotten you. For wherever I found Truth, there I found my God, the Truth itself, and since I learned that, I have not forgotten it. So then, since I learned you, you have lived in my memory, and there I find you when I call you to mind and take delight in you. These are my holy delights, which you have given me in your mercy, looking upon my poverty.

But where in my memory do you live, Lord — where do you live there? What kind of dwelling have you made for yourself there? What kind of sanctuary have you built for yourself there? You have granted my memory the honor of your dwelling in it, but in which part of it you dwell is what I am now considering. For in thinking of you, I passed beyond the parts of it that even beasts have, since I did not find you there among the images of bodily things; and I came to the parts where I had stored the feelings of my mind, and I did not find you there either. And I entered into the very seat of my mind — which it holds in my memory, since the mind also remembers itself — and you were not there either; for you are not a bodily image, nor a feeling of a living being, such as we have when we rejoice, grieve, desire, fear, remember, forget, or the like. And so you are not the mind itself either, because you are the Lord God of the mind, and all these things change, while you remain unchangeable over all of them — and yet you have chosen to dwell in my memory ever since I learned you. And why do I go on asking in what part of it you dwell, as if there were places in it at all? I am certain that you dwell in it, since I have remembered you ever since I learned you, and there I find you when I call you to mind.

Where, then, did I find you, so that I could learn you? For you were not in my memory before I learned you. Where, then, did I find you, so that I could learn you, if not in you, above me? There is no place involved here — we move backward and forward, and there is no place. Everywhere, O Truth, you give a hearing to all who seek your counsel, and you answer all of them at once, even though they ask your counsel on many different matters. You answer clearly, though not everyone hears clearly. Everyone consults you about whatever they wish, though they do not always hear what they wish. Your best servant is the one who looks not so much to hear from you what he himself wants, as rather to want what he hears from you.

Too late I loved you, O Beauty so ancient and so new, too late I loved you! And look — you were within, and I was outside, and it was there that I searched for you; and I, deformed, went rushing about among the beautiful things you had made. You were with me, and I was not with you. Those things kept me far from you, things which, unless they were in you, would not have existed at all. You called, and cried out, and broke through my deafness. You flashed, you shone, and you drove away my blindness. You breathed your fragrance on me, and I drew in my breath, and I pant for you. I tasted you, and now I hunger and thirst for you. You touched me, and I burned for your peace.

When I cling to you with my whole self, I will have no more sorrow or toil anywhere, and my life will be wholly alive, wholly full of you. But for now, since you lift up the one you fill, and I am not full of you, I am a burden to myself. Joys I should mourn wrestle with sorrows I should welcome, and on which side victory lies, I do not know. Woe is me! Lord, have mercy on me. My bad sorrows wrestle with my good joys, and on which side victory lies, I do not know. Woe is me! Lord, have mercy on me. Woe is me — look, I do not hide my wounds; you are the physician, I am the sick one; you are merciful, I am wretched. Is the life of man on earth not entirely a trial? Who wants troubles and hardships? You command us to endure them, not to love them. No one loves what he endures, even though he may love to endure it, for even if he is glad that he endures, he would rather there were nothing for him to endure at all. In adversity I long for prosperity, in prosperity I fear adversity. What middle ground is there between the two, where the life of man is not entirely a trial? Woe to the prosperities of the world, once and again, from fear of adversity and the corruption of joy! Woe to the adversities of the world, once and again, and a third time, from the longing for prosperity, and because adversity itself is a hard thing, and because it might shatter endurance. Is the life of man on earth not entirely a trial, without a single break?

And all my hope is nowhere but in your immense mercy. Give what you command, and command what you will. You command us to be continent, and when, as one man said, I knew that no one could be continent unless God gave it, this too was itself a part of wisdom, to know whose gift it is. Through continence, truly, we are gathered back and bound together into one, from the many pieces into which we had been scattered. For a man loves you too little who loves anything alongside you that he does not love for your sake. O love, ever burning and never consumed! O charity, my God, set me on fire. You command continence — give me what you command, and command what you will.

You truly command me to be continent from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the world. You command continence from illicit sex, and even for marriage itself, you have advised something better than what you have permitted. And since you gave me this, it was already accomplished even before I became a minister of your sacrament. But there still live in my memory — which I have spoken of so much already — the images of things my bad habit fixed there, images that still haunt me, though powerless when I am awake; but in sleep they not only give pleasure but even win consent, something very close to the real act. Indeed, the illusion of the image prevails so completely, in my soul and in my flesh, that when I am asleep, false visions persuade me of what, when I am awake, the true things cannot. Am I not, then, myself, Lord my God? And yet there is so much difference between myself and myself, within that very moment in which I pass from waking to sleeping, or return from sleeping to waking! Where is reason then, the reason that resists such suggestions while awake? And even if the real things themselves were pressed upon it, it would remain unshaken. Is it shut off along with the eyes? Is it put to sleep along with the senses of the body? And how is it that often, even in sleep, we resist, and, mindful of our purpose, hold to it most chastely, giving no consent to such enticements? And yet there is enough difference that when it happens otherwise, on waking we return to peace of conscience, and by this very difference we discover that we did not do what we are nonetheless sorry was somehow done in us.

Are you not mighty, God Almighty, mighty enough to heal all the diseases of my soul, and by your still more abundant grace to quench even the impure stirrings of my sleep! You will increase your gifts more and more in me, Lord, so that my soul may follow me toward you, freed from the birdlime of desire, so that it does not rebel against itself, and so that even in dreams it not only refrains from these degrading corruptions, working through images of sense all the way to defilement of the flesh, but does not even consent to them. To bring this about — that nothing of this kind should have even the smallest influence over the pure affections even of someone asleep, no more than a mere thought would be able to restrain — is not hard, not only during this life but even at my present age, for the Almighty, who is able to do far more than we ask or think. But what I still am in this respect of my sinfulness, I have confessed to my good Lord, rejoicing with trembling in what you have given me, and mourning over what in me is still incomplete, hoping that you will bring your mercies to completion in me, all the way to perfect peace, which my outward and inward self will have with you, when death is swallowed up in victory.

There is another evil belonging to the day, which I wish were enough on its own. For by eating and drinking we repair the daily wearing away of our bodies, until you destroy both belly and food, when you will put my emptiness to death with a wonderful fullness, and clothe this perishable body with an eternal imperishability. But for now this necessity is sweet to me, and I fight against that very sweetness, so as not to be taken captive by it, and I wage a daily war through fasting, often bringing my body into subjection; and my pains are driven off by pleasure. For hunger and thirst are, in a way, pains; they burn and destroy like a fever, unless the medicine of nourishment comes to our aid. And since that medicine is at hand, through the comforts of your gifts, by which land and water and air serve our weakness, our calamity is given the name of gratification.

This you have taught me: that I should set myself to take food the way one takes medicine. But while I am passing from the discomfort of emptiness to the contentment of being filled, the snare of desire lies in wait for me in that very passage. For the passing itself is a pleasure, and there is no other way to pass through to where we must necessarily go. And since health is the reason for eating and drinking, a dangerous pleasure attaches itself to it as a companion, one that mostly tries to go ahead of health itself, so that I end up doing for its sake what I say — or think — I am doing for health's sake. Nor do the two have the same measure, for what is enough for health is too little for pleasure. And it is often uncertain whether it is the necessary care of the body that is still asking for nourishment, or whether a voluptuous deceitfulness of greed is offering its services instead. In this uncertainty my unhappy soul takes a kind of comfort, and in it prepares an excuse to shield itself, glad that it does not appear clearly what is sufficient for the moderate care of health, so that under the cloak of health it can disguise the business of gratification. These temptations I try to resist every day, and I call on your right hand, and refer my confusions to you, because I have as yet no settled policy about this.

I hear the voice of my God commanding: Do not let your hearts be weighed down with excess and drunkenness. Drunkenness is far from me; you will have mercy, so that it never comes near me. But full feeding sometimes creeps up on your servant; you will have mercy, so that it stays far from me. For no one can be continent unless you give it. You give us many things when we pray for them, and whatever good we received before we prayed, we received from you — and it was so that we might later come to know this, that we received it even before we asked. I have never been a drunkard, but I have known drunkards made sober by you. From you, then, it came that those who were never drunkards should not become so, just as it was from you that those who had been drunkards should not remain so; and from you it was that both should know from whom it came. I heard another word of yours: Do not go after your desires, and turn away from your pleasure. And, by your favor, I have heard something I have loved very much: neither if we eat shall we have more, nor if we do not eat shall we lack anything — which is to say, the one will not make me rich, nor the other miserable. I heard also another: I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content with it; I know how to have abundance, and I know how to suffer need; I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me. Here is a soldier of the heavenly camp, and not the dust that we are. But remember, Lord, that we are dust, and that you made man out of dust, and that he was lost and is found. Nor could he have done this of himself, because he whom I so loved, when he said this through the breath of your inspiration, was made of the same dust. I can do all things, he says, through him who strengthens me. Strengthen me, so that I can. Give what you command, and command what you will. He confesses to having received, and when he boasts, he boasts in the Lord. I have heard another begging that he might receive: Take from me, he says, the desires of the belly — from which it appears, my holy God, that you give, when what you command to be done is actually done.

You have taught me, good Father, that to the pure all things are pure, but that it is evil for a man to eat with a guilty conscience; and that every creature of yours is good, and nothing is to be refused that is received with thanksgiving; and that food does not commend us to God; and that no one should judge us in food or drink; and that whoever eats should not look down on the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat should not judge the one who eats. These things I have learned — thanks be to you, praise to you, my God, my Teacher, knocking at my ears, enlightening my heart — deliver me out of every temptation. I do not fear the uncleanness of food, but the uncleanness of craving it. I know that Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh that was good for food, that Elijah was fed with meat, that John the Baptist, gifted with a remarkable abstinence, was not defiled by feeding on living creatures, the locusts. I also know that Esau was deceived by his craving for lentils, and that David blamed himself for wanting a drink of water, and that our King was tempted not concerning meat but concerning bread. And so the people in the wilderness also deserved reproof, not for desiring meat, but because, in their desire for food, they grumbled against the Lord.

Placed then amid these temptations, I struggle daily against desire in eating and drinking. For this is not something I can decide to cut off once and for all and never touch again, the way I could with sex outside marriage. So the bridle on the throat must be held in a balance between slackness and severity. And who is there, Lord, who is not carried at least a little beyond the limits of what is necessary? Whoever he is, he is a great man; let him make your name great. But I am not such a man, for I am a sinful man; yet I too magnify your name, and he who has overcome the world makes intercession to you for my sins, counting me among the weak members of his body, because your eyes have seen what is still imperfect in me, and in your book all shall be written.

With the enticements of smells, I am not much troubled. When they are absent, I do not miss them; when present, I do not refuse them; and I am always ready to be without them. Or so it seems to me — perhaps I am mistaken. For there is a mournful darkness in me too, by which my own abilities are hidden from myself, so that my mind, questioning itself about its own powers, does not readily trust what it finds — because what is in it is mostly hidden, unless experience brings it to light. And no one ought to feel secure in this life, the whole of which is called a trial, since the one who has been able to change from worse to better could just as easily be changed from better to worse. Our only hope, our only confidence, our only sure promise, is your mercy.

The pleasures of the ear had entangled and mastered me more firmly, but you loosened their hold and set me free. Now, in the melodies that your words breathe life into, when sung with a sweet and well-trained voice, I do rest a little — not so as to be held fast by them, but so that I can free myself whenever I wish. But along with the words that give them life, and by which they gain entry into me, they seek out some place of honor in my feelings, and I can hardly assign them the right one. For at times I seem to myself to give them more honor than is fitting, sensing that our minds are raised more devoutly and more fervently into a flame of devotion by the holy words themselves when they are sung this way than when they are not, and that the different feelings of our spirit have their own proper measures in the voice and the singing, through some hidden correspondence by which they are stirred. But this pleasure of the flesh, to which the soul must not surrender itself to be weakened, often deceives me, when the sense does not simply accompany reason patiently but, having been let in only for reason's sake, tries instead to run ahead of it and lead it. In this way I sin without noticing, and only afterward become aware of it.

At other times, guarding too anxiously against this very deception, I go wrong in the opposite direction, into too great a strictness — sometimes to the point of wishing that the whole melody of the sweet music used for David's Psalter were banished from my ears and from the Church's too; and the practice that seems safer to me is the one I remember being told about often, concerning Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, who had the reader of the psalm recite it with so slight an inflection of voice that it was closer to speaking than to singing. And yet again, when I remember the tears I shed at the singing of your Church, in the early days of my recovered faith, and how even now I am moved, not by the singing but by the things that are sung, when they are sung with a clear voice and the most fitting melody, I recognize the great value of this practice. So I waver between the danger of pleasure and the proven benefit of it, inclined rather — though not pronouncing an unchangeable opinion — to approve the custom of singing in church, so that through the delight of the ears weaker minds may be raised to a feeling of devotion. Yet when it happens that I am more moved by the voice than by the words being sung, I confess that I have sinned in a way that deserves punishment, and at such times I would rather not hear the singing at all. See now my condition — weep with me, and weep for me, all of you who regulate your own feelings so that good actions follow from them. For those of you who do not act on it, these things do not touch you. But you, Lord my God, listen; look, and see, and have mercy and heal me — you, in whose presence I have become a puzzle to myself, and that is my weakness.

There remains the pleasure belonging to these eyes of my flesh, on which I must make my confessions in the hearing of the ears of your temple, those brotherly and devout ears, and so bring to a close the temptations of the lust of the flesh that still assail me, as I groan deeply, longing to be clothed with my dwelling that comes from heaven. The eyes love beautiful and varied shapes, and bright, soft colors. Let these not take hold of my soul; let God take hold of it instead, God who made these things — very good indeed, yet he is my good, not they. And these things affect me all day long while I am awake, and I am given no rest from them, as I sometimes have from music, in silence, from all voices. For this queen among colors, the light, bathing everything we look at, wherever I am through the day, slips past me in its many forms and soothes me even while I am occupied with other things and not paying attention to it. And it winds itself around me so tightly that, if it is suddenly taken away, it is sought after with longing, and if it stays away long, it saddens the mind.

O that Light which Tobit saw, when, though his own eyes were closed, he taught his son the way of life, and himself went ahead with the feet of charity, never wandering. Or the Light which Isaac saw, when, his fleshly eyes heavy and closed with old age, it was granted him, without knowing it, to bless his sons — and by blessing them, to come to know them. Or the Light which Jacob saw, when he too, blind through great age, with an illumined heart, shed light in the persons of his sons on the different peoples of the future, foreshadowed in them, and laid his hands, crossed in a mystical way, upon his grandsons through Joseph, correcting them not as their father would with his outward eye, but as he himself discerned inwardly. This is the Light; it is one, and all who see it and love it are made one in it. But that bodily light I spoke of seasons the life of this world for its blind lovers with an enticing and dangerous sweetness. Yet those who know how to praise you for it — "O Lord, maker of all things" — take it up into your hymns, and are not taken up by it in their sleep. Such would I be. These seductions of the eyes I resist, so that my feet, with which I walk your way, may not be caught in a snare, and I lift up my unseen eyes to you, so that you would pull my feet out of the trap. You draw them out again and again, for they are constantly caught. You never stop drawing them out, while I keep tangling myself in the snares laid on every side — because you, who keep Israel, will neither slumber nor sleep.

What countless trinkets, made by all sorts of arts and crafts, in our clothes, shoes, furnishings, and every kind of work, and in paintings too and various images — things that go far beyond any necessary or moderate use, and beyond any devout purpose — have men added to tempt their own eyes with, outwardly chasing after what they themselves have made, while inwardly abandoning the one by whom they themselves were made, and destroying what they themselves have been made to be! But I, my God and my Glory, sing a hymn to you even out of this, and I dedicate praise to the one who dedicates me, because those beautiful patterns which pass through men's souls into their skillful hands come from that Beauty which is above our souls, the Beauty my soul sighs after day and night. But those who shape and those who follow after outward beauties draw from that Beauty their rule for judging them, though not their rule for using them rightly. And he is there, even though they do not perceive him, so that they might not wander off, but might keep their strength for you instead of scattering it abroad on pleasures that only wear them down. And I, even though I say this and see it, tangle my own steps in these outward beauties; but you pull me out, Lord, you pull me out, because your loving-kindness is before my eyes. For I am caught wretchedly, and you pull me out mercifully — sometimes without my even noticing, when I had only lightly brushed against them, and at other times with pain, because I had stuck fast in them.

To this is added another kind of temptation, dangerous in even more ways. For besides the desire of the flesh, which lies in the delight of every sense and pleasure, and by which its slaves, wandering far from you, waste away and perish, the soul has, through those same bodily senses, a certain vain and inquisitive desire — cloaked under the name of knowledge and learning — not a desire to take pleasure in the flesh, but a desire to run experiments through the flesh. Since its seat is in the appetite for knowledge, and sight is the sense chiefly used for gaining knowledge, it is called in the language of Scripture the lust of the eyes. For, strictly speaking, seeing belongs to the eyes, and yet we use this word for the other senses too, whenever we use them in the pursuit of knowledge. We do not say, listen how it flashes, or smell how it glows, or taste how it shines, or feel how it gleams, for all these are said to be seen. And yet we say not only, see how it shines, which only the eyes can perceive, but also see how it sounds, see how it smells, see how it tastes, see how hard it is. And so the general experience of the senses, as I said, is called the lust of the eyes, because the function of seeing, in which the eyes hold the leading place, is taken over by the other senses, by a kind of resemblance, whenever they go searching after any knowledge.

But by this we can more clearly tell apart what makes pleasure the object of the senses, and what makes curiosity their object; for pleasure seeks out things that are beautiful, melodious, fragrant, tasty, soft, while curiosity, just to test them, seeks out the opposite as well — not for the sake of suffering discomfort, but out of a desire to make trial of things and to know them. For what pleasure is there in looking at a mangled corpse, something that will make you shudder? And yet if one is lying nearby, people flock there, to be made sad and to turn pale. Even in their sleep they are afraid to see such a thing. As if, when awake, anyone forced them to look at it, or any report of its beauty drew them there! It is the same with the other senses too, which it would take too long to go through one by one. It is from this disease of curiosity that all those strange spectacles put on in the theater come. From it, men go on to search out the hidden powers of nature — which lies outside our proper end — knowledge that profits nothing, and in which men want nothing but to know. From it too, if pursued with that same aim of perverted knowledge, come the magical arts. And from it too, even in religion itself, God is put to the test, when signs and wonders are demanded of him, not desired for any good purpose, but merely to make trial of him.

In this vast wilderness, full of snares and dangers, look — I have cut off many of these things, and driven them out of my heart, as you have granted me, God of my salvation. And yet, since so many things of this kind buzz around our daily life on every side, when would I dare to say — when would I dare to say that nothing of this sort engages my attention, or stirs in me an idle interest? It is true the theaters no longer carry me away, nor do I care to know the courses of the stars, nor has my soul ever consulted the spirits of the dead; I detest all sacrilegious rites. From you, Lord my God, to whom I owe humble and single-hearted service, by what tricks and suggestions does the enemy work on me to want some sign! But I beg you, by our King, and by our pure and holy homeland, Jerusalem, that just as any consent to such a thing is far from me now, so may it be pushed ever further and further away. But when I pray to you for someone's salvation, my purpose and intention are very different. You give, and you will go on giving, that I follow you willingly, doing what you will.

Still, in how many small and contemptible things is our curiosity tempted every day, and how often we give in — who could count them all? How often do we start out as though merely tolerating people telling pointless stories, so as not to offend those weaker than us, and then, little by little, find ourselves taking an interest in them! I no longer go to the circus to watch a dog chasing a hare, but if I happen to pass one in the countryside, that chase might well distract me even from some serious thought and draw my attention after it — not that I turn my animal's body aside, but my mind still leans that way. And unless you, having made me see my own weakness, quickly warn me either to rise toward you through some reflection on the sight itself, or else to despise it entirely and pass it by, I stand there dully, fixed on it. What about when, sitting at home, a lizard catching flies, or a spider tangling them as they rush into her web, often catches my attention? Is it any different just because these are small creatures? I move on from them to praise you, the wonderful Creator and Orderer of all things, but that praise is not what first draws my attention. It is one thing to get back up quickly, another thing not to fall at all. And my life is full of such things, and my one hope is your wonderful, great mercy. For when our heart becomes a storeroom for such things, and is weighed down with crowds of this abundant emptiness, our prayers too are often interrupted and scattered because of it, and while in your presence we direct the voice of our heart toward your ears, this great concern of ours is broken off by the rush of I know not what idle thoughts. Are we, then, to count this too among things of little importance, or is there anything that can bring us back to hope, except your complete mercy, since you have already begun to change us?

And you know how far you have already changed me — you who first healed me of the desire to justify myself, so that you might forgive me all the rest of my wrongdoing, and heal all my weaknesses, and redeem my life from ruin, and crown me with mercy and pity, and satisfy my desire with good things — you who curbed my pride with your fear, and tamed my neck to your yoke. And now I carry it, and it is light for me, because you have promised this, and you have made it so; and truly it was so, though I did not know it when I was afraid to take it up.

But, Lord, you alone are Lord without pride, because you are the only true Lord, the one who has no lord over him — has this third kind of temptation also ceased in me, or can it ever cease through this whole life? I mean the wish to be feared and loved by men for no other reason than to have a joy in it that is no true joy at all? This is a miserable life, and a shameless kind of boasting. It is chiefly from this that men fail to love you or fear you in a pure way, and so you resist the proud and give grace to the humble; indeed, you thunder down upon the ambitions of the world, and the foundations of the mountains tremble. Because certain duties of human society now make it necessary to be loved and feared by men, the enemy of our true blessedness presses hard upon us, everywhere spreading his snares of "well done, well done" — so that, greedily snatching at them, we may be caught off guard, and split our joy off from your truth and set it instead in the deceitfulness of men, and be pleased at being loved and feared not for your sake but in your place; and so, having been made like him, he may have them for his own, not through the bonds of love but through the bonds of punishment — he who set out to place his throne in the north, so that, dark and cold, they might serve him, in a twisted and crooked imitation of you. But we, Lord, look — we are your little flock; possess us as your own, stretch your wings over us, and let us fly beneath them. Be our glory; let us be loved for your sake, and let your word be feared in us. Whoever wants to be praised by men when you find fault will not be defended by men when you judge, nor delivered when you condemn. But when — not when the sinner is praised for the desires of his soul, nor the one blessed who acts wickedly, but — when a man is praised for some gift that you have given him, and he takes more pleasure in the praise for himself than in having the gift for which he is praised, he too is being praised while you are being slighted; and better is the one who gave the praise than the one who received it. For the one took pleasure in the gift of God in a man; the other was better pleased with the gift of man than with the gift of God.

By these temptations we are assailed daily, Lord — without ceasing we are assailed. Our daily furnace is the tongue of men. And in this too you command us continence. Give what you command, and command what you will. You know, on this matter, the groans of my heart and the floods of my eyes. For I cannot tell how far I have been cleansed from this plague, and I fear greatly my hidden sins, which your eyes know and mine do not. For with other kinds of temptation I have some means of examining myself; with this one, scarcely any. For in restraining my mind from the pleasures of the flesh and from idle curiosity, I can see how much progress I have made, when I do without them — either giving them up, or simply not having them. For then I ask myself how much more or less troublesome it is to me not to have them? But wealth, which is desired to serve one or two or all three of these forms of desire — if the soul cannot tell, while it still has wealth, whether it despises it, then wealth can be set aside, so that the soul may test itself that way. But to be without praise, and to test our strength in that condition — must we live badly, indeed so shamelessly and monstrously, that no one could fail to detest us? What greater madness could be spoken or imagined? But if praise does and should go along with a good life and good works, we ought no more to give up its company than to give up the good life itself. And yet I do not know whether I can be without something well or badly, unless it is actually absent.
