What then do I confess to you in this kind of temptation, Lord? What, except that I am pleased by praise — but more pleased by the truth itself than by praise? For if it were put to me whether I would rather, raving in error about everything, be praised by all men, or, steady and firmly settled in the truth, be blamed by all, I can see which I would choose. And yet I wish that another person's approval did not even increase my joy over some good thing in me. But I admit it does increase it, and not only that — disapproval lessens it too. And when I am troubled by this weakness of mine, an excuse occurs to me, and what it is worth, you, God, know, for it leaves me uncertain. Since you have commanded us not only continence — that is, from what things to hold back our love — but righteousness too, that is, on what to bestow it, and have willed us to love not only you but our neighbor as well, often, when I am pleased by intelligent praise, I seem to myself to be pleased by my neighbor's progress or promise, or grieved over some fault in him, when I hear him find fault with either what he does not understand, or what is good. For sometimes I am grieved at my own praise, either when the things praised in me are things I dislike in myself, or when even lesser and slighter good qualities are valued more highly than they should be. But again, how do I know whether I am affected this way only because I would not want the one who praises me to disagree with me about myself — not out of concern for him, but because the same good things that please me in myself please me more when they please someone else too? For in a sense I do not feel praised at all when my own judgment of myself is not praised, since either the things praised are ones that displease me, or the things that please me less are praised more. Am I then uncertain of myself in this matter?

Look — in you, Truth, I see that I ought not to be moved by praise of myself for my own sake, but for the good of my neighbor. And whether that is how it is with me, I do not know. For in this matter I know less of myself than I know of you. I ask you now, my God, uncover me to myself as well, so that I may confess to my brothers, who are to pray for me, where I find myself crippled. Let me examine myself again more carefully. If, when praised, I am moved by concern for my neighbor's good, why am I less moved when someone else is unjustly criticized than when it is myself? Why am I more stung by blame cast on myself than by blame cast on someone else, with the same injustice, right in front of me? Do I not know this either? Or is it, in the end, that I am deceiving myself, and not doing the truth before you in my heart and on my tongue? Keep this madness far from me, Lord, lest my own mouth become, for me, the sinner's oil that fattens my head. I am poor and needy, yet best off when, in hidden groans, I am displeased with myself, and seek your mercy, until what is lacking in my defective state is renewed and made complete, reaching that peace which the eye of the proud does not know.

Yet the word that comes out of the mouth, and deeds known to men, carry with them a most dangerous temptation through the love of praise, which, in order to build up some excellence of its own, courts and collects the votes of men. It tempts even when it is rebuked by myself in myself, on the very ground that it is rebuked, and it often boasts more emptily of the very contempt of empty glory — and so it is no longer contempt of empty glory that it boasts of, since it does not truly despise what it boasts of.

Within, too — within is another evil, arising from a similar temptation, by which men become vain, pleased with themselves in themselves, even though they do not please others, or displease them, or do not care whether they please them. But in pleasing themselves, they greatly displease you — not only taking pleasure in things that are not good as though they were good, but even in your good things as though they were their own; or, if they credit them to you, still as though they had earned them by their own merit; or even if they credit them to your grace, still not with a brotherly rejoicing, but begrudging that grace to others. In all these dangers and struggles, and others like them, you see the trembling of my heart, and I feel my wounds being healed by you far more than I feel them not being inflicted by me in the first place.

Where have you not walked with me, O Truth, teaching me what to guard against and what to desire, when I brought before you whatever I could discover here below, and consulted you about it? With my outward senses, as best I could, I surveyed the world, and observed the life that my body has from me, and these senses of mine. From there I entered the recesses of my memory, those vast and many-roomed chambers, wonderfully stocked with countless treasures, and I considered them, and stood in awe, being able to make out nothing of these things without you, and finding none of them to be you. Nor was I myself the one who discovered these things, who went over all of them and labored to distinguish and to weigh each thing according to its worth, taking some things on the report of my senses, questioning others which I sensed as mixed in with myself, numbering and distinguishing the reporters themselves, and, in the great treasure house of my memory, turning some things over, storing up others, drawing out others. Nor was it I myself who did this, either — that is, the power by which I did it — nor was it you, since you are the abiding light which I consulted about all these things, whether they existed, what they were, and how they were to be valued, and I heard you directing and commanding me; and this I often do, this delights me, and, so far as I can be freed from necessary duties, I turn to this pleasure. Nor, in all the things I go through in consulting you, can I find any safe place for my soul except in you, where my scattered parts might be gathered, and nothing of me might depart from you. And sometimes you allow me an experience, quite unlike the usual, deep within my innermost self, rising into a strange sweetness, which, if it were made complete in me, I do not know what there would be in it that would not belong to the life to come. But through my miserable burdens I sink back down into these lower things, and I am swept back by old habit, and I am held fast, and I weep greatly, but I am held fast all the same. So heavily does the weight of a bad habit press down on us. Here I am able to stay, but do not want to; there I want to be, but cannot; both ways, I am miserable.

So then I have considered the sicknesses of my sins in that threefold desire, and have called your right hand to my aid. For with a wounded heart I have looked upon your brightness, and, driven back, I said, "Who can reach up to that? I am cast away from the sight of your eyes." You are the Truth who presides over all things, but I, through my own greed, wanted not to lose you but to possess a lie along with you — just as no one wants to speak falsely in such a way as to be himself ignorant of the truth. So then I lost you, because you do not allow yourself to be possessed together with a lie.

Whom could I find to reconcile me to you? Was I to turn to the angels? With what prayers? With what sacraments? Many people, trying to return to you and unable to do it on their own, have, as I hear, tried this, and fallen into a longing for strange visions, and been judged worthy to be deceived by them. For, being proud-minded, they sought you through the pride of learning, puffing out their chests rather than beating their breasts, and so, by the agreement of their hearts, drew to themselves the princes of the air, fellow conspirators in their pride, by whom, through magical powers, they were deceived, while seeking a mediator through whom they might be purified — and there was none. For it was the devil, transforming himself into an angel of light. And it was a great enticement to proud flesh that he had no body of flesh. For they were mortal, and sinners; but you, Lord, to whom they proudly sought to be reconciled, are immortal and without sin. But a mediator between God and man must have something in common with God and something in common with men — for if in both respects he were merely like man, he would be too far from God, and if in both respects he were like God, he would be too unlike man, and so would not be a mediator at all. That deceptive mediator, then, by whom, in your hidden judgments, pride deserved to be deluded, has one thing in common with man — sin — while he wants to seem to have another thing in common with God: since he is not clothed with the mortality of the flesh, he boasts of being immortal. But since the wages of sin is death, this he has in common with men — that with them he is condemned to death.

But the true Mediator, whom in your hidden mercy you showed to the humble, and sent, so that by his example too they might learn that same humility — that Mediator between God and man, the man Christ Jesus, appeared between mortal sinners and the immortal Just One: mortal with men, just with God — so that, because the wages of righteousness are life and peace, he might, through a righteousness joined to God, do away with the death of sinners now made righteous, the death he chose to have in common with them. This is why he was shown to holy men of old, so that they, through faith in his Passion still to come, just as we through faith in it already past, might be saved. For as man, he was a mediator; but as the Word, he was not in the middle between God and man, because he was equal to God, and God with God, and together one God.

How you have loved us, good Father, who did not spare your only Son, but gave him up for us who were ungodly! How you have loved us — for whom he who did not think it robbery to be equal with you was made subject even to death on the cross, he alone free among the dead, having the power to lay down his life and the power to take it up again — for us, before you, both Victor and Victim, and therefore Victor because he was the Victim; for us, before you, Priest and Sacrifice, and therefore Priest because he was the Sacrifice; making us sons instead of servants to you, by being born of you and serving us. My hope, then, rests strongly in him, that you will heal all my weaknesses, through him who sits at your right hand and makes intercession for us; otherwise I would despair. For many and great are my weaknesses, many and great — but your medicine is mightier still. We might have supposed your Word to be too far removed from any union with man, and have despaired of ourselves, if he had not been made flesh and dwelt among us.

Terrified by my sins and the burden of my misery, I had turned it over in my heart, and had resolved to flee to the wilderness; but you forbade me, and strengthened me, saying: Christ died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them. See, Lord, I cast my care upon you, so that I may live, and may consider the wonders of your law. You know my lack of skill and my weaknesses; teach me, and heal me. Your only Son, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, has redeemed me with his blood. Let not the proud speak evil of me, because I meditate on my ransom, and eat and drink it, and share it with others; and, poor as I am, I long to be satisfied by him, among those who eat and are satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him.
